Mr. Speaker, it would not seem to be necessary to spend very much time on this bill, having regard to the fact that everyone seems to ibe desirous of sending it to a committee. So possibly the proper time to speak would be after the findings of the committee are brought before the house. Nevertheless a number of suggestions were made this afternoon that might be helpful to the committee, and I might possibly be fortunate enough to contribute some more. I am going to try to keep away from the tone of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) yesterday. Of course we feel entirely forgiving towards him because it shows he has been able to stage his come-back, as it is called. I hope he does not overdo it; we are all very
anxious about his health. As the leader of one of the great parties we want to see him in good condition when he lines up for battle.
It gives us more freedom in discussion, and besides we do not like to see any hon. gentleman of his standing and capacity only half well. I hope however not to continue the somewhat meat-axe style of discussion with which he challenged this side of the house yesterday.
I am going to run over briefly some of the government's blundering record in dealing with wheat. I am not going to be harsh, but they have developed a penchant that when they put their hands into the wheat problem they usuallv put their foot in it at the same time. That was quite manifest when the government first endeavoured to give a bonus of 5 cents per bushel. They attempted to give a much needed five cent bonus to the farmers of the west, and first proposed to distribute it through the medium of the railways, somehow absorbing it in their freight rates. The next proposition was to give it through the exporters. Some of us could not see how it would ever reach the farmer through that medium, and as it was ostensibly meant for him we made some candid criticisms of the method. Finally the government brought on Mr. Ramsay and he made a plan of distributing this five cent bonus based on the same policy as the 1919 wheat board adopted. That should have been known to the government, but apparently the then Minister of Trade and Commerce had forgotten the old method. We have been roundly blamed for opposing that bonus, and blamed no doubt in connection with the bonuses given since, simply because we criticized and showed how it could be done to better advantage and more effectively.	.
The next government move was the Sir Josiah Stamp commission dealing with wheat futures, although the preceding government had bah an investigation into wheat futures by Mr. Justice Turgeon who dealt with that same question very completely and came to much the same conclusion as did Sir Josiah Stamp and his commission. But the government could not get even that simple thing done without putting their foot in it, and they did so by inserting what was called appendix 12. I do not know how it got in-, inadvertently, it was said. I have a good guess how it got in, but I am not sure. At that time the government did not seem to be quite as friendly with the wheat pool as they are now, because this appendix 12 certainly gave the pool and their general organization a jab in the short ribs that they felt. How-
Grain Board,-Mr. Motherwell

ever after some discussion on the subject the government decided to call in all those wheat future reports about a thousand I think, and have that offending appendix removed. I think if we knew all the story about that distorted appendix it would take half an hour to tell it.
Then we had the Prime Minister going over to London in 1930 to try out his blasting methods of selling farm produce. We do not need very long to deal with that; he came home empty handed and the conference was adjourned to Ottawa at a subsequent date. It was to be within a year but it proved to be nearly two. I shall not dwell on that incident except to recite very briefly the great expectations that were aroused in the west as the Prime Minister came home. He arrived in this city; he was not banqueted if I remember rightly, because that was the occasion on which he came back empty handed, but the newspapers had him paged at every divisional point between here and Regina; a telegram went forward that the Prime Minister was one day's journey nearer the prairies, where he was going to give a message of great encouragement to the expectant farmers. Rut that was the greatest frost in which the Prime Minister ever figured; he had nothing to tell them, and he told it well.
Then we had the Ottawa conference of 1932, right in this building, and the famous six cent preference which was not meant to give us any more money for our wheat; it was to hit the other fellow. I do not think much of that way of doing business; hitting the other fellow does not do us much good. We do not hear much about that now, except that the foreigner with his depleted currency seems to have got the inside track of us. They have been hit and they thought we in Canada were responsible. The Prime Minister indicated on more than one occasion that the intention was not to make the mother country pay six cents more for our wheat but to give us a sheltered market. Is it a sheltered market now? From what? Not the Argentine, we rather are sheltering the Argentine.
Then there came the international wheat sonference; that was another dud. I think oerhaps the government meant well, but there vas some preliminary spade work that, in my estimation, required to be done before they could ever hope to have a successful international wheat conference that could reach any conclusions that would be binding. We had grossly offended Russia, a great country starting out on its own line of government, which they had a right to do no matter what we might think of it. This 
federal government took authority at the very first session, and exercised it the second session, to embargo six or seven of Russia's major export commodities. At one time that would have been a sufficient international offence to cause war, but our government did not seem to have any hesitation in engaging in that kind of dangerous heroics. This international wheat conference was the aftermath of a great international conference that met in London in 1933, and not having accomplished much, this subsidiary conference was called, with our Prime Minister as chairman, of some twenty or twenty-one countries which import or export wheat. From that kind of setting how could one expect anything worth while? Argentina is blamed for breaking away from the quota agreement arrived at there. Russia never did sign the agreement so far as the quota was concerned. I do not see how we can blame Argentina very much when we never had this agreement submitted to this parliament for its approval. It never got the formal endorsation of this parliament, so any other country could well hide behind that well known fact and make it an excuse for defaulting. However, this international wheat committee has still a continuing committee, bumming around and drawing their salaries and affording some excuse for the government hanging on to another of their marketing illusions until after the election. Mr. Andy Cairns, the great statistician, and the gentleman who is credited with advising the wheat pool wrongly regarding the withholding of the full measure of grain sales which _ might have been made in 1929 and 1930, is Canada's representative on the international continuing wheat committee. So that that is another dud exploded. It has become a habit with hon. members oipposite to make blunders in connection with the disposing of wheat and dealing with wheat problems.
We come now to the wheat debacle of 1929 and 1930. It will be recalled that in February, 1930, or therabouts, the three provincial governments guaranteed the banks against, loss on wheat pool operations. They had the misfortune of making their initial payments too large. I hope the government will take cognizance of that fact and will not indulge in that procedure when this wheat board is in operation, unless it is intended to bonus that way. The fact developed that the three western wheat pools had paid out to contract signers over $22,000,000 more than was coming to them. It was impossible to get that large amount back so they entered into a statutory agreement with the Saskatchewan government to have the loan paid back in

Grain Board-Mr. Motherwell
nineteen equal annual instalments. Up to this date I am pleased to report that all payments have been met on due dates. Apparently at that time the banks did not have much confidence in the wheat pool situation, and because of that they wanted further security and obtained it from this government.
At this point Mr. McFarland entered) into the picture. I have a lot of sympathy for him because he took on an impossible job. When the Prime Minister introduced the resolution in March of this year I do not know how he knew that Mr. McFarland was going to be sick. However if the account of his speech which I read1 in the Ottawa Journal was correct and from what I heard of it mySelf I would gather that this bill is predicated upon the assumption that Mr. McFarland is too ill further to give his sendees to the country as chairman of the selling agency. How did the Prime Minister know at the time he introduced the resolution three months ago that Mr. McFarland was going to be sick? He could not have known. Mr. McFarland has delivered at least two outstanding addresses, one in Winnipeg in April and another in Regina in May, since the resolution was brought down, and showed himself in good form.
I should be interested to learn whether or not the Prime Minister has acquired the art of foretelling and foreseeing other people's health. He does not answer. I think that was just a little fairy tale; he forgot himself. He must have forgotten his resolution forecasting this bill, and he gave the only reason he could think of at the time, namely that Mr. McFarland was in poor health and would not be in a condition to carry on further stabilization operations, hence this bill. I believe it is a compliment to the Prime Minister to observe that he cannot think up a better fairy tale than that one, and it shows that he is not an adept at telling yams. Therefore I shall con- -elude my remarks on this phase of the matter by complimenting him. He would ten times rather tell the truth than quibble even a little bit. However, he forgot himself, he forgot the resolution was on the order paper at least three months before the bill was introduced, and at a time when Mr. McFarland's health was good enough to enable him to give good public addresses.
I have said that when Mr. McFarland was asked by .means of stabilization to give to the farmers a much needed bonus on their wheat prices, he was asked to do an impossible task as sales would drop off if such bonus were passed on to our overseas customers. It was proposed by the Prime Minister that the
bonus which could be given under the stabilization policy would equal the five cent original bonus that was cancelled at the end of 1931. I believe the house will recall that the Prime Minister indicated one would almost equal the other. It would appear to me that at times the stabilization operations exceeded the five cent bonus and was appreciated accordingly.
Speaking at Moose Jaw in February last before the Saskatchewan school trustees' association Air. McFarland gave the story of his appointment, and told why he was working without salary. Part of his speech is as follows:
He was wholly in accord with my action. I was offered any reasonable salary

I presume by the pool or by the government, I do not know which.
-I cared to name, but I refused to accept the position on a salary basis-
Matk you.
-because it was a national emergency, and I was well aware that the greatly overexpanded world production of wheat was such that no man could accomplish or expect to accomplish that necessary perceptible measure of success as would warrant a salary.
He admitted he was not able to do this job of giving a bonus to the farmers on top of the normal wheat price, and at the same time sell wheat to the world in competition with comparable wheats of other countries. What did he do? He put up the price and sold it to our complaining customers across the seas at prices frequently running from eight to twelve or more cents higher than the usual premium accorded our wheat. In other words, through the stabilizing agency, by giving a bonus, and making the customers abroad pay for it, the Canadian government were making good fellows of themselves with the farmers. They did that, instead of taking that money out of the coffers of the country and paying it direct, as they did when they paid the five cent bonus of 1931. They thought they were devising a cute way of doing things; they were playing a cheap racket and paying bonuses, but making our customers on the other side of the ocean pay enhanced prices. That is the story. No wonder Mr. McFarland said he would not undertake such a task and that he could not give value for a salary. As I am not corrected in any of these details I assume I am stating the accepted facts. Mr. McFarland admitted beforehand that the task he had been given was an impossible one. The government has found it so, and that is the reason this bill is before us.
Grain Board-Mr. Motherwell

Same bon. members on this side of the house have been represented as being opposed to bonuses. I believe most people would like to get away from them, but when you have the secondary classes in a community with their feet in the trough, what are you going to do with the others? Can you keep them out? No, you cannot play favorites in a crisis such as this. I have always felt some disappointment in the secrecy and furtiveness with which the government's stabilization policy has been surrounded. If the Prime Minister feels justified in complaining about a whispering campaign, why during all these years has he withheld the information from us and left the public to guess the wheat holdings of Mr. McFarland, and other important details? Why didn't he come out and tell us the facts and then the people would not have had to do any guessing? I have for at least two years right in this parliament objected to this star chamber method of handling the greatest export commodity of the country. There is no justification for it under the sun, and either it shows a disposition to want to cover up something or they did not know enough about the business to know that other wheat-bonusing countries were revealing the facts of their sales month by month. As I recall, in the United States the late Alexander Legge made no bones about what was going on in the United States, and he very soon got from under.
May I refer to the Commercial Intelligence Journal issued under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) and his deputy minister, Mr. Parmelee. Under date of January 12, 1935, the Commercial Intelligence Journal at page 50 carries an article by Mr. Scott, a Canadian trade commissioner, on Board of Control for Cereals in Argentina. It is an amazing thing, Mr. Speaker, that the government will hand out all this information without any hesitation not only in this issue of the Commercial Intelligence Journal 'but in another publication to which I shall refer in a moment, telling all and sundry what is being done in the Argentine and then refrain for four and a half years from telling us anything about the Canadian situation except what was told us last night as to the volume of wheat in the selling agencies' hands. Here is the statement on page 50:
Following the announcement that the same basic prices would be continued for the coming season, a separate statement has subsequently been issued reporting on the operations of the grain board between December 4, 1933, and

November 26, 1934. The statement shows that the operations of the grain board during the above-mentioned period have been carried on at a total loss of around 8,815,000 paper pesos.
A peso is about 53 cents, so that amounts to about 14,000,000:
The loss sustained by the grain board in maintaining minimum prices has, however, been fully covered by the profits made by the government in the buying and selling of foreign exchange.
The Argentine is also giving bonuses to their farmers. The Argentine people go further into the business and gamble in foreign exchange, and they put up their profits on that against their losses on wheat sales. But our government wants to make our [DOT]customers pay for the bonuses to farmers, thus driving them elsewhere for their wheat supplies. They have something to learn yet, and I think this committee could do a whole lot of good if we had the time to do it, but Mr. McFarland is in hospital and we had the Prime Minister in effect telling us last March in the resolution that Mr. McFarland was going >to be sick today, and possibly could not come down here to give evidence. I hope That the committee will assemble in a very different spirit from that in which the Prime Minister addressed the house last night, and I am glad that I have sufficient self-control not to follow suit in the meat ax fashion that he then adopted.
Referring again to the Commercial Intelligence Journal, here is a table giving the monthly purchases, sales, cancellations, and stocks for the different months of the year; for instance, purchases for the month pf December amounted in round figures to 571,000; sale$, 28,000; cancellations, 3,000; stocks, 540,000, and so on. The figures are given for every month of the year. But not a word from this government. They have been as silent as the grave. Of course, they knew they were approaching their political graves and perhaps that suggested the silence. But is that the way to do business? This government that preaches ethics in business violates every decency of ethics in connection with our wheat business, and there is no one who does it more than the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce. We will get around to him later on perhaps.
Here is a note about these cancellations, and those of us who have conscientious scruples about the compulsory features will note this:
The figures given under the heading of cancellations represent sales made to the board which were subsequently cancelled by the seller when able to dispose of bis grain more advantageously elsewhere.

Grain Board-Mr. Motherwell
I support my hon. friend fronm South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) in the remark he made just before six o'clock when he recommended, as I recommend, that the Argentine policy of handling their wheat sales be studied carefully by the committee so far as time will permit, and this know-all government will find something to learn there. The people of the Argentine have learned how to bonus their farmers and yet sell their wheat,-something not yet learned by Canada.
Here is a very interesting document which is gotten out every month by this government, by the Department of Trade and Commerce, called the Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation. We can get all kinds of information about the Argentine. Just see what they say on page 25 of the issue for March, 1935:
The correspondent of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in the Argentine has forwarded' the following report under date of March 4, 1935.
That is the correspondent of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in the Argentine. I would presume they have a resident correspondent there. I do not know whether he is a special correspondent or not. At any rate he is the correspondent of this government, whether an employee I do not know, but I would expect not. He says:
One of the features of the market during the month has been the brisk demand for Barusso wheat from Bahia Blanca territory. Of the various types of Argentine wheat this is the one which most nearly approximates that of Canada. Hence it is much in demand by millers as a substitute for Canadian wheat now that that is being practically held off the market by the high prices asked for it, and buyers are quite willing to pay a premium over the prices of other Argentine types, even the Rosafe which was formerly the leader here.
There is this correspondent making this admission in this document issued by the government, and I presume it is correct, that now that Canadian wheat is largely off the market because of high prices the people of the Argentine are selling their wheat quite freely in place of ours. I think it was no wonder Mr. McFarland got sick, carrying such a load of anxiety and responsibility in the attempt to do the impossible, as previously indicated.
Another issue of the Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation published by the Minister of Trade and Commerce says on page 11 under the heading, Grain Control Board:
Just as the month of November closed, the ministry of agriculture gave publicity to the long-expected statement as to the operations of the grain control board in respect of wheat.
They were anxious to hear about it, and apparently the information had been delayed
for a few months. What if it had been delayed for four and a half years? The article continues:
Up to November 28 the official board has sold 138,756,000 bushels, having still on hand a remnant of 6,142,000 bushels.
That is all they had over.
The total expenses of the board amounted to 8,814,942 paper pesos of which 5,881,756 represents the loss on the grain sold; 2,455,000 interest money borrowed for the purpose of its operations-
And so forth. No trouble about getting information about other parts of the world, but we who supply the line of credit could not get a peep out of this government until last night, and then only a meagre statement of what we knew already, that there was approximately 200,000,000 bushels of wheat futures in the hands of Mr. McFarland. The country all along knew it. The grain men on the exchange day by day can make an estimate of how much the government or, aa it is called, the pool agency, holds, so why the secrecy? Why has the government tried to keep this a secret? They must have had some object in mind but they cannot put it over on us by saying it was for the public interest-it was for their own interest, otherwise they would never have dared the criticism of the public for doing business in the clandestine way they have been doing it for the last four years and a half. There is nothing else but to send this bill to the committee and make the best of a bad business of losing markets in these dying days of a dying government. I am in favour of referring this bill to a committee for possible improvement, and I shall reserve my further remarks to a discussion of the findings of that committee.
Farmers were faced not only with the difficulty of having their wheat down to the lowest price it had been for four hundred years but they also had to compete with a monetary system where the currency of the Argentine was away down below ours. Those of us who sold five bushels of No. 1 northern for $1 and less at the point of shipment in December, 1932, know the crucifixion we had to go through; I sometimes wish the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his colleagues were personally aware of that so they would know the agonies the farmers had to suffer. What the government should have done was to go off the gold standard at the time Great Britain went off and not continue to crucify us on our export sales with a low British pound which had to be converted into high Canadian dollars.
It will be remembered that about this time last year I tried for four months to get a

copy of a report made by Sir Herbert Marler, Canada's representative in Tokyo, Japan. I cannot understand the argument of the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), nor can I understand the arguments of other hon. members who are growing wheat in my province. Reference was made this afternoon to the wheat pool, and I think I am right when I say-the former Minister of Agriculture can correct me if I am wrong-that he was in favour of the wheat pool. I believe the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) was also in favour of this pool. I think they will agree with me when I say that the object in the first place was the orderly marketing of wheat. I will not go back to conditions as they existed prior to the time we organized the pools, but I can remember very well that the wheat growers sent down a deputation -in fact more than one deputation-when hon. gentlemen now in opposition were in power, about the year 1922, asking them to reinstate the wheat board. And I can infer from the fact that they did not do so that the farmers of western Canada found it necessary to organize the pools. We were very anxious to have the old board reinstated because we felt that it was to the advantage of the farmers to have this done, and when it was not done it was decided to organize the pools. Hon. gentlemen who are now criticizing this bill so severely should bear in mind that they refused to give us the wheat board, and therefore there was nothing for us to do but to organize the pools. I believe that Alberta took that step in 1923 and we followed in 1924. We went into that business for the express purpose of having the grain marketed in an orderly way;
that was the object in organizing the pools.
I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to say that the policy of the government in the last three or four years, or under Mr. McFarland, if you will, has not been for that same purpose, namely, to provide orderly marketing. What else is it? It amazes me to hear hon. gentlemen advocating the dumping of our wheat on the markets of the world, to the extent that they have suggested to-day.
I do not wonder so much when I hear that proposal coming from the hon. gentleman who has been acting as critic for the opposition, because he is a lawyer; but I am surprised to hear farmers from western Canada advocating it. They know very well that round about 1923 or 1924 we found it absolutely necessary to take the action we did then, and I am borne out in this by what the Prime Minister said yesterday. When wheat production began to go up, increasing to hundreds of millions of bushels, what else could we have done? I have been thirty years growing wheat in the west and I can remember when our exports amounted to less than one hundred million bushels. But when they got up to three and four hundred million bushels, the farmers of western Canada deoided that the time had come for a change of policy so far as the grain exchange was concerned, because they could not save the situation. The volume had increased to such an extent that we were obliged to make our own market, and that is why we went in for orderly marketing.
The hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) this afternoon condemned the wheat pools; this attitude is characteristic of him. The total carryover for 1929 was 127,000,000 bushels, and the pool's proportion of that was 52,000,000 bushels. In other words, the western pools carried forty per cent of the carryover while the trade carried sixty per cent.

speechtext:
The bill
now before the house to establish a grain board is a measure which I think a majority of the farmers of western Canada have looked forward to for a number of years. Wheat has now become distinctly a national problem, and I do not think it can be dealt with effectively except through a national agency. In fact wheat is not only a national problem, it is an international problem. Most of the nations of the world have gathered together in conference several times in recent years to discuss it. It may be these conferences have not been successful, but the very fact that all these countries thought it necessary to hold such conferences and take part in them should impress upon us the gravity of the problem.
No country in the world is more concerned in the wheat problem than Canada. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) pointed out yesterday, we have been the largest exporter of wheat in the world. The importance of the industry to Canada was so well stated by the Prime Minister yesterday 'that there is no necessity for me to do more than mention it. Wheat is not only a national problem but the wheat problem has now become a national responsibility. I should like to take a few minutes to try to prove that fact to the house. I say it is a national responsibility, first because of the national immigration policy which has been in force in Canada from 1896 until 1913, with the exception of the war period. The policy has been to bring as many farmers as possible to Canada, to settle them on the western prairies and to push the wheat acreage as far north as possible. In the period between 1922 and 1929, particularly, the organized farmers of western Canada protested against this policy, and I remember that in 1923 I stated in this house that the greatest danger facing western Canada was that of overproduction, or producing more than we could, sell at a profit. I remember being questioned in the lobby by one of the Conservative members, and being asked whether or not I was sincere in that statement. He thought I was only talking for political effect, and when I assured him I was sincere he simply laughed and said, "You're crazy." The time seems to have arrived when we have produced more than we can sell at a profit. As a matter of fact that time arrived a few years ago. Between pre-war years and 1933 the wheat acreage in Canada increased by 161 per cent. We had a percentage of increase in wheat acreage greater than that of any other country. Surely the nation cannot

Grain Board-Mr. Coote

disclaim responsibility for this; it was a direct result of government policy. There was the policy of immigration coupled with that of the development of new wheats so that the wheat acreage could be pushed farther north.
I remember a few years ago the former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who preceded me to-night with an excellent speech, stated he looked forward to the time when Canada would produce a billion bushels of wheat.

The statement has been made, anyway. The extension of the wheat area and the increase in acreage was responsible for the increased volume of production, and that was the outcome of a distinctly national policy.
The present problem of the farmer is one of price, and to some extent at least price is the result of another national policy. I now refer to the problem of the exchange value of Canadian money, a point which I believe was raised this evening by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). Our chief competitors, as is well known, are the Argentine and Australia. Our difficulty in connection with the price of wheat has arisen in the last five years. Prior to that time we did not have much difficulty, with the exception of some odd years, in obtaining a fair price. The internal price, namely, the price to the producers in Canada, during most of the time- perhaps not during the last year-has been lower than the price paid to our competitors in their own countries and in their own currency. The internal price to our producers is dependent largely on the amount of Canadian funds we have been able to secure for foreign funds for which our wheat was eventually sold. Late in the year 1929, by government action, the Argentine abandoned the gold standard and devalued or depreciated their currency, thereby raising to the Argentine producer the price of wheat as expressed in paper pesos. Their internal currency is the currency in which their debts are expressed, and the currency with which they buy their requirements in the Argentine. In January, 1930, about a year later, Australia abandoned gold redemption and devalued her currency

in the same way. The fact is that it depreciated very rapidly. For the past five years the pound sterling has been at a premium of twenty-five to thirty per cent in Australia; most of the time I believe it has stood at twenty-five per cent. Hon. members will recall that in the fall of 1932, when wheat was at its lowest point in Canada, the pound sterling in Canada was worth about $3.70 to $3,75. At the same time the pound sterling was at a premium of twenty-five per cent or was worth approximately $6 in Australia. At that time the Australian competitor had a sixty per cent exchange advantage over the Canadian producer. Had our currency then been at par with Australian wheat, on the worst day in 1932, instead of being worth 38J cents I believe our wheat would have been worth at least 60 cents Fort William, in Canadian currency. That would have happened without any change in the world gold price for wheat.
I have not the figures to indicate the exact exchange situation in the Argentine at that particular time, but since January, 1930, their currency has been at least as low as and sometimes lower than it has been in Australia. At the moment I am not placing the blame for this policy on any persons. It is sufficient for my purpose to state that on many occasions hon. members in this corner of the chamber have urged that our currency be brought down to the level of Australian currency. On those occasions we received very little support from either the government or the opposition. In the fall of 1932 the opposition did support us in a proposal that the pound sterling be brought up to a parity in Canada. With that exception however I cannot remember having received any support from either side of the house, nor did we receive any from the financial authorities in Canada, namely, the heads of banks and other large financial institutions.
The point I wish to make clear is that it was the national policy of Canada to. keep our currency at a high value in New York, and keeping our currency at that high value had the effect of forcing down the value of the British pound in terms of Canadian currency until, as I have said, in the fall of 1932 it was at one time as low as $3.70. That was the result of a national policy. I have indicated that by our policies of immigration, the development of Wheat areas in western Canada and our stand on monetary matters we have in the last few years created a problem for the wheat grower. I believe the

Grain Board-Mr. Coote
nation must assume the responsibility fox dealing with it.
Mosit of the increase in wheat prices we have at the present time is due to the depreciation of the pound sterling in terms of gold, coupled with the fall of our dollar to the level of the pound. This latter factor, namely the fall of our dollar, was due to a change in the money policy of the United States. I should like again to emphasize the point that we should take whatever action is necessary to give the farmer a reasonable price for his wheat, and that the nation should assume whatever financial risk may be involved in meeting the problem. For the benefit of the house may I point out that the agitation for a wheat board in western Canada has gone on for many years, dating back to the wheat board which operated during the last year of the war. In 1922 or 1923 legislation passed this chamber to establish a wheat board, but the action was taken very late in the season and as we were told it was found impossible to get. proper management the matter was allowed to drop. As long as I have been in western Chnada there has been a feeling that the selling of our wheat on the grain exchange was not the best method of disposing of it. I believe in response to feeling whibh had developed in western Canada, in 1931 the so-called stamp commission was appointed to inquire into the question of selling our wheat on the grain exchange. The report indicated an approval of the present system, but inside of eighteen months the system had absolutely broken down and wheat reached its lowest level of 38| cents. Not long after the Stamp commission had reported, Mr. Richardson of the Winnipeg grain exchange was before our agriculture committee advocating that the government should support the market. The government has been supporting the market for the last few years, and experience has proven that it is very difficult and expensive. We have not only had to support the legitimate hedges of the elevator companies to cover deliveries at country elevators, but we have also had to protect the market against the short selling of .millions of bushels of futures. We understand this short selling came from the United States, and dear knows where else. We do not really know where it all came from, but I have heard that in one day alone orders for as much as ten million bushels of short sales came on the Winnipeg market and had to be taken care of or the market would have broken, and many farmers would have had to let their wheat go at a very low price indeed. There were at all times speculators who were willing to break the market if they thought they could do it, but 92582-2304
the speculator that we depended upon to support the hedges seems to have disappeared. As one man in western Canada said to me, he has become almost as extinct as the dinosaur, and because there is no speculative interest to take up these hedges I feel that it is imperative that a wheat board should be set up.
It seems to me that under the old system it was no one's particular business to sell our wheat. We always seemed to take it for granted that Canadian wheat would sell itself. I have been told that the grain trade looked after that. The grain trade are largely interested in the elevator business; so long as their elevators were filled with wheat they were sure of storage charges, and I never could believe that they were desperately keen to get all this wheat sold and shipped out because once the wheat was shipped out the storage charges, and of course their earnings, would cease.
I repeat, I am in favour of this bill to establish a grain board, but I would also like to make it clear to the house that the board must have the financial, assistance from the nation which will enable it to pay a fair price to the producer even if it has to sell the wheat to the world at a lower price. I believe that in the national sense it would pay us to guarantee to our producers a price covering the cost of production and to sell the wheat at the best price we can obtain. In this connection I would like to draw the attention of the members to the example that has been set by the Argentine. I quote from the Monthly Commercial Letter issued by the Canadian Bank of Commerce for the month of May, 1935. With reference to the operations of the Argentine grain board it says:
In November, 1933, the Argentine government set up a grain marketing board to assist producers. Its chief functions were to set a basic price for -wheat, flaxsed and corn, to purchase such grain at the fixed price and to sell it for export only at the prevailing world price. As the world price was lower than the basic price the government would have had to absorb a possible heavy loss. This difficulty was overcome, with the cooperation of the exchange control board, by lovrering the rate at which the peso was pegged (it was already at a discount of about 40 per cent below its gold parity) and utilizing the resulting exchange profits to cover any loss on the grain board's operations. The board calculated at the outset that it might incur a loss of fifty million pesos, which would have to be recovered from exchange profits. A rise in prices_consequent on the drought last year in the United States, however, reduced the subsidy per bushel to a relatively small sum, and to the end of Sep-fember. 1934, a substantial net profit was realized on the whole operation, which it was
Grain Board-Mr. Coote

planned to use in financing the next season's crops. It is important to note that the board claims that in buying grain as it was offered, and regulating its sales to demand, it avoided breaking the world market with abrupt offerings of Argentine grain.
Apart from the success which it achieved in disposing of all but a very small carryover of the large 1933-34 crop at a price satisfactory to growers and at no loss to itself, the grain board has undertaken to mitigate, and hopes eventually to remove, the two disabilities under which the Argentine grain trade is still operating, namely, the production of a large volume of certain varieties of wheat not readily acceptable by importers, and lack of elevator and storage space.
I would like to commend this method of financing the operations of the board to the study of the committee which I understand is to consider this grain board bill. I also wish to quote the concluding paragraph of the Monthly Letter of the Canadian Bank erf Commerce dealing with the Argentine's method of handling wheat. It says:
We can no longer blind ourselves to the intensity of the competition Canadian wheat is meeting from Argentine, nor can we dismiss it as a temporary phenomenon. Argentina is now the world's leading exporter of grains, and is making every effort to consolidate her position. She has met and overcome difficulties just as great as those with which Canada now contends, and provides an example of enterprise and resolution in dealing with them.
In conclusion, I hope that we may show ;he same enterprise and resolution in dealing with the problem of marketing Canada's wheat. I trust that when this bill goes to the committee which I understand is to consider it, it will be dealt with expeditiously and thoroughly and that a plan may be evolved under which the Canadian producer may be guaranteed at least the cost of production for his crop, and that the very best possible methods may be provided for the sale of our wheat to all the buyers we can find anywhere in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have taken a great deal of interest in this bill ever since it was introduced because I have been growing wheat in Canada for the last thirty years, and of necessity anything in connection with wheat is of great interest to me. As I sat here and listened to different members talking about wheat my mind went back to 1930, to the time of the election, and I thought of the way Conservative speakers throughout the country spoke on every platform at that time and told us of the wonderful prices we were going to get for agricultural products of all kinds if they were elected. Butter, why that was spread over every platform. Wheat, why it was then at one dollar a bushel, and we were 
told that we were going to get $1.50 a bushel at least. We were told that just as soon as the Conservative party got into power the price of wheat was going to rise in ten days by ten cents a ibushel at least. But no sooner had the Conservative party got into power than wheat began to go down, and it went down and down until we thought i.t would never stop.
As I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) yesterday I thought of what was said on almost every platform in 1930 in connection with' wheat. Quoting the Liberal Minister of Trade and Commerce, Conservative speakers said:
The Department of Trade and Commerce is not exercised over the sale of such commodities as wheat because those commodities find their own markets.
That was the statement made by the Liberal Minister of Trade and Commerce in those days, and it was repeated from practically every platform in western Canada. Now in those days we never thought of finding a market for our wheat. As my hon. friend from MacLeod (Mir. Coote) has just said, we believed in those days that wheat would find its own .market all over the world. And it was finding its market. I would ask the Prime Minister now what he would have done a/t-that time when we had ia carryover of only
127,000,000 fousheiLs, which was nothing at aill compared with the carryover we have had for the last four years? Would he have recommended that the government take it over and sell it? He would not have recommended anything of the kind. They used that as a sort of argument to throw up as a screen. Every step taken by this government in connection with wheat has 'been a mistake. They have made one error after another and there is not one move they have made in connection with wheat which has been, right. Shortly after the Prime Minister was elected he went over to London. He returned and came out to Regina .and the word went over the western prairies that the Prime Minister had a story to tell us. The Premier of Saskatchewan sat on the platform with him to introduce him to his audience, and the rest of us were listening at our radios to hear his message. What did he tell us? He told us he had a market in France, but where is that market? I am surprised that there is such a carryover. What has become of the market he claimed he had found? AVe do not hear anything about that market now. Have we lost it? Then he told us that at that moment the ambassador to Japan was on his way to China to find a market for our wheat in that country. Where has that market gone to? Apparently

Grain Board-Mr. Donnelly
the Chinaman has gone back to eating rice altogether. These are some of the things this government has done.
What next? What happened after those faux pas? He then started the five cent wheat bonus. As the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has said1, the Prime Minister was first going to pay this bonus on export wheat; then it was to be paid on the freight on wheat; then he brought the grain commissioner to Ottawa to talk things over and he decided to pay it to the growers of wheat when they brought in their wheat for sale. What did that mean? It meant that the man who had wheat received a bonus of five cents per bushel while the man who had none had to pay more for his flour and bread. We in the southern part of the province got nothing; we did not get one of the nickels he was talking about. The man who had the wheat got more while the man who had no wheat got less, even that which he had was taken away. The man who was hailed out, the man who was frozen out, the man who was dried out and the man who was eaten out by the grasshoppers got nothing, but the man who had a crop received five cents a bushel. This was done to stimulate production and urge the farmers to grow more wheat. That was a mistake.
What was the next thing? The next thing was to bring a man over here to look into the grain trade. Something was wrong with that trade and it had to be straightened out. Sir Josiah Stamp was brought over and he stamped everything. He told us the grain exchange was all right and that it should be kept up as a means of marketing our wheat. Now the Prime Minister turns around and presents a bill to do away with the exchange. Did you ever see such a series of contradictions? Ohe thing right after another. Sir Josiah Stamp said that we needed the grain exchange; the Prime Minister brings a great economist over here to tell him that and then he turns around and says we do not need it and he presents a bill in order to do away with it. The government is going out of power and they will not be here to see this bill put into effect. The government will be lucky to be the official opposition after the next election. They know that they will not be here to see that this bill is Carried out and so they are going to put it through.
What next did1 they do? The next thing was the Ottawa agreements. We were told that these would settle all our difficulties, that we would get into the English market without having to pay any duty on our wheat
while the Argentine and other countries outside the empire would have to pay six cents a bushel. I can still hear the Prime Minister telling us about these agreements. He told us that there would be two ships lying side by side at the quay of one of the ports of old England, one from Canada and the other from some other country. The wheat in the ship from Canada would go in free while the other ship would not be permitted to unload its wheat until it had paid six cents a bushel. One would have imagined that all the wheat consumed in England would be going there from Canada and Australia, but what do we find? In 1932 the Argentine sold 19-5 million bushels of wheat; in 1933 they sold 21-9 million bushels and in 1934 they sold 34-2 million bushels. In two years there was a gain of 15 million bushels. What about Canada? Perhaps I had better give these figures under my breath. In 1932 we sold 44-4 million bushels of wheat to England; in 1933 we sold only 40-6 million bushels and in 1934 only 34-7 million bushels. Our sales have dropped 10 million bushels. We were given an advantage of six cents a bushel; this was a sheltered market which was going to solve all the difficulties of the wheat growers of western Canada.
Then when they saw that that was not going to work, they went to Rome to try to reach an agreement. They consulted with France fault France replied that she was willing to reduce her duties and her restrictions against our wheat if we told her what we would buy from her. Was any one sent from here to try and make an agreement with France whereby we would take something in exchange for our wheat? No; nothing was done.
They then adjourned to London and a lawyer was sent from the prairies to sell- our wheat. He went over there with all expenses paid and then we were told that the only thing to do was to put on a quota. We were told we would have to cut down our acreage as we were growing too much wheat. Can you imagine going down into the southern part of Saskatchewan where they have not had a crop for six years and telling the farmers they are growing too much wheat? The former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) made reference to the program of recovery in the United 'States under the NRA and its system of codes. Instead of a blue eagle he suggested to the government that they should adopt the grasshopper as their emblem. The grasshopper will cut down the acreage and get rid of a lot of wheat. The drought and the hail will get rid of a lot of wheat.
Grain Board-Mr. Donnelly

No one kept these quotas, and in fact our government loaned part of our quota to the Argentine. We are wondering when we will get that back. It is all just a faroe because no one is adhering to the quota. This is just something else put through in an effort to deceive the farmer. The party opposite have done nothing else but try to deceive the farmers in one way or another ever since they got into power, and even before. That is the way they got in and that is the way they are going to slide out; make no mistake about that.
Now, having done all these things and having done them all wrong, and having made mistakes in everything, they said, "The thing to do is to stabilize the price; you have to get a man there." And so they put in this man McFarland to stabilize the price. In season and out of season for the last four years, both in the committee and in the house, I have tried to find out something of their activities, but I have not been able to discover anything. The first bit of information which we got was given us the other night by the Prime Minister, namely, that we have 200,000,000 or 226,000,000 of a carryover, held by Mr. John I. McFarland for Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. But what it has or has not cost the country we do not know.
I have said before, and I say again tonight, that this government is gambling in wheat. That is denied. When they buy futures, that is not gambling-oh, no; that is only supporting the market. But when I buy futures, or when anyone else buys futures, it is gambling, it is speculating. Listen to this from the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who talks so glibly about trade ethics and all that kind of thing:
The hon. member who took his seat a few minutes ago said that this government was guilty of gambling in wheat, and that we had lost $30,000,000. No statement could have been further from the fact than that. This government is not either directly or indirectly gambling in wheat.
Note that-not either directly or indirectly gambling in wheat; yet we have 225,000,000 bushels.

The hon. member for Melville made the same statement the other night. What this government has done is this. It has supported Mr. McFarland, who was chosen as their manager by the pool selling agency for the three western pools. The government has stood behind that

selling agency, controlled by Mr. McFarland', in taking care of wheat futures on the Winnipeg market. What does that mean?...
Anybody who knows anything about business knows that if a government were to disclose its hand day by day in regard to these things, it would have ruined the 'wheat market.
He does not mean the wheat market; he means the government. And surely it would ruin the government, because if they told the public that they were gambling in wheat, they know what the result would be. And what do we find on top of that? The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), discussing this question the other night, told us that in that year 1933 Mr. McFarland sold something like 20,000,000 or 30,000,000 bushels, and it was being sold then in the neighbourhood of 80 or 90 cents. Later on he bought back all the wheat he had sold1-I wonder why. The Prime Minister said that the only reason Mr. McFarland bought it back was that prices had not been maintained. Let me quote from Hansard of March 13, 1934, page 1545, what the right hon. gentleman said:
Prices have not been maintained at a fixed level but rather they were supported, particularly during the season of the year when farmers were, from necessity, forced sellers of their production in order to meet the demands and needs of their creditors.
This was in July, but no farmer was selling his wheat at that time to meet the demands of his creditors; it was not done for that purpose at all. During that year we sold
372.000.	000 bushels-that is, in October for the crop year 1932-33-and the average price for the eleven months was 51f cents. That was the average for the eleven months beginning the first of August, 1932, to the first of July, 1933. We had sold 359,000,000 bushels at an average price of 51J cents, and then during the month of July the price went up and it averaged 83 cents a bushel. And that was the very time, when the price went up, that Mr. McFarland stepped in and sold. It went as high as 94 cents, and when he saw it coming down again he bought back the
20.000.	000 bushels he had sold. Why? Was that gambling? Of course it was. He thought it would go up to $1; that was rumoured all over the country. He was buying, thinking he would get an extra price; but the 20,000,000 bushels he had sold he bought back. He bought back every bushel he sold, and all the wheat that came in from the country during that month of July was 13,000,000 bushels. Why was he doing that? He was doing it for no other purpose than to speculate; he was gambling in wheat. We are told that it was a matter of supporting the market. Well, when you buy anything you are supporting the market; anyone knows that who

Grain Board-Mr. Donnelly
has anything to do with wheat. When you are buying you are speculating and you are supporting the market. But the Prime Minister knew that he was doing that; he knew that Mr. McFarland was gambling in wheat. He must have known it because before the banking and commerce committee Mr. McFarland was questioned and he said, as reported at page 236 of the evidence:
Mr. Bennett knew what was being done from time to time; he had the reports. The banks reported to him the position from time to time.
The Prime Minister knew that Mr. McFarland was gambling in wheat; there is no doubt about it. The next point I wish to refer to with regard to this gambling process is this, and it shows how many contradictions there are in the minds of members of the government. One of the things the Prime Minister said was that he would never set a price. I have sat in this house and listened to members opposite condemning the wheat pool just because, as they said, they had lost the market by setting the price higher than it should be. I have listened to member after member discussing the pool and pointing out how they had held the price up. Listen to what the former Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as reported at page 1742 of Hansard of May 14, 1931:
In the fall of 1929-30 a condition arose in Europe which was really an attitude of resentment rightly or wrongly, against the North American continent in regard to wheat. Rightly or wrongly they conceived the idea that to their detriment we were attempting unduly to advance the price of wheat. Hearing that rumour the European buyers turned their purchases in other directions. For instance, the Argentine got a very distinct advantage, and further we found that many of the flour mills in the consuming countries of Europe-Holland', Germany, Belgium, Switzerland, and X think, France-had changed or readjusted their screens so as to mill the Argentine wheat instead of ours. Then this year we found that millers in those countries were very reluctant to change their screens back again.
And use the old screens so that they could use Canadian wheat. The hon. member said at the same time:
In the meantime recognizing that situation we have been doing our best to carry it and to disabuse the minds of the European people of the thought we had any intention of cornering the wheat market.
Referring to nobody but the western pools; that they were the ones that had lost our markets and that they had done wrong in trying to uphold the price. Then the Prime Minister himself,, as reported on page 782 of Hansard of April 21, 1931, said this:
Practically one-half of that wheat was held by the pools of the country.
This government got behind those pools and said it would assist the orderly marketing of the wheat crop of western Canada. That assistance and support had, of course, the same effect upon non-pool wheat. That was what the government did. It did not peg the price; no government of which I ,am the head ever will.

Did hon. members hear that "hear, hear"? I wonder what Mr. McFarland has done if he has not pegged the price. The Prime Minister continued:
I have seen artificial prices placed upon commodities and whether that commodity be wheat or anything else, it matters not, I know the inevitable result. It cannot advantageously be done; it will not succeed. It may Cause a temporary advantage but that disappears. Look at the situation in the United States to-day. Mr. Legge, with all his vast experience, with all the millions and hundreds of millions of dollars that he had behind him, declared that the principle of artificial pricefixing was unsound, and it has been abandoned. We did not adopt it, so we did have to abandon it.
Speak about contradictions! It has been just one contradiction after another. As regards everything they have attempted to put over, they have turned around, changed their minds and done something else. As the former Minister of Agriculture said, they have stepped into every hale from Vancouver to Halifax; there is no doubt about that. Now they are beginning to take great credit to themselves because they have set the price. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) spoke of thirty cents a bushel as having been saved. Some of them say that 1100,000,000 has been saved to western Canada and some of them have mentioned as high as $200,000,000. By the time of the election it will be up to $500,000,000; it is growing day by day and by leaps and bounds. I say: Go back to western Canada; stand up on the platforms there and ask the farmers to put their hands into their pockets and feel that thirty cents a bushel, that $100,000,000, that $200,000,000, you people have saved for them and you will be sure to get their votes; do not make any mistake about that! In my opinion, if hon. members opposite are depending upon that to get the votes 'Of the western producers, they are depending upon a broken reed, a rotten stick.
Consider what this policy has done for the people of western Canada, especially those in the southern part where I come from. We have had no crop whatever for six years. The government say that they have kept the price up; some hon. members mentioned thirty cents a bushel, and the result has been
Grain Board-Mr. Donnelly

that we have lost our markets; iwe are not selling our wheat. Every other country in the world has sold its wheat, but we are left holding the bag. The Argentine has got rid of all its wheat; Australia has got rid of all hers and so has the United States; we are the only country with any surplus of any account. We are holding the bag. Our people, thanks to Providence, expect to get a crop this year; weather conditions are good and they believe they will have a crop. The only thing this government has done for them in the past is to make them pay more for their seed, more for their flour, more for their feed, because if what my hon. friends opposite say is right-and I presume it is- they have kept the price up. Now our people have around their necks a millstone of
200,000,000 bushels of wheat preventing them from getting a price for their crop when they see one in sight this year. That is a great help to them. Let my hon. friends visit the southern part of Saskatchewan and tell the farmers there these stories as well as the others.
I say this: If you want to keep up the price and to bonus wheat, all well and good. You have bonused all kinds of industries in this country. We do not believe in bonuses; we do not think any industry or any article should be bonused; but if you are going to bonus all the industries, the farming industry should be bonused also. But I say. Sell the wheat; get rid of it; clear out our bins and let us get a world price. When this government goes out of power, as it will as soon as the election comes along, and we put proper policies into effect in this country, the farmers will be able to sell their wheat, but at the present time I believe a board is necessary. A board should have been appointed long ago, one that would tell us from day to day, from week to week or from month to month what is being done. We were not complaining when they were bonus-ing the farmers, when they were bonusing everything else; we were not condemning the wheat pools or anything else, but we were condemning the way in which the government was acting, this clandestine secret way of doing things, with no one knowing what was being done, and then the government expecting us to support it when no one knew what it was he was supporting. Is it any wonder we want to know now what the government activities are, how much it is out of pocket now, how much this policy is going to cost us? Now the government comes along and brings us this wheat board. What for? To bury the old corpse; that is all;

to bury its mistakes in regard to its stabilized wheat policy. The government found itself with 220,000,000 bushels of wheat that will cost us we do not know how much and it wants to bury this in the new board. That is what the government expects to do, and that is why it is coming now in the dying days of the session with this kind of bill, this kind of proposition. It wants to appoint a board to bury this corpse, this doctor's mistake it has made.
So far as I am concerned I welcome this board if for no other reason than that it will bring about publicity. I do not think it will be necessary to have it for more than a year; I think it should be appointed only from year to year. We want to get away from it as soon as possible because it is only a false, a mistaken way of doing things. It may be necessary in order to clean up this mistake. What is the government going to do with this 220,000,000 bushels of wheat? How is it going to handle it, sell it, if not through a board? Of course the government has to have a board to sell that quantity of wheat. Why leave it to one man? Is it any wonder he is sick in bed to-day trying to carry a load of this kind, trying to market all this wheat, taking all the load upon himself, then trying to sell this wheat, make a profit and get away with it? We would never have heard a word about the matter if there had been a short crop this year. The government talks about excessive crops. Since the government came into power we have never had a crop that was more than an ordinarily fair crop; 1933 was the only year we had anything but half a crop in western Canada. This year we might likely have a crop of
600,000,000 bushels. What is the government going to do with it? When it sees this ahead of it and knows it is coming, it brings in this board and makes it carry the load.
I intend to support the principle of this bill; I support the principle of a board, a board to handle it instead of one man. Whether the bill when it comes from the committee is amended in such form that I can support it on third reading remains to be seen.

After hearing from the opposition a man does not need to speculate as to the source from which the Liberal party expect to receive their campaign funds. But the question which we as members of this house must consider when this bill comes up for third reading is, are we going to sacrifice seven hundred thousand farmers to greed and exploitation? That is what has been going on in this country the last fifty years. I hold that as representatives of the people we cannot sit by and let this thing go on any longer; if we do we fail in our duty to the people who sent us here. That is the way I feel at any rate, and I represent a very large farming constituency. As to the grain exchange in Winnipeg, it is just too bad we are going to sacrifice that. When I drive around Wellington Crescent and down by the river and see the great mansions there, all taken out of the sweat and blood of the farmer, as far as I am concerned I find very little difficulty in deciding on which side I am going to line up. I am going to support this bill with all that I have.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth said he did not think anyone in western Canada was in favour of this bill. I wonder if he heard the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) today, the president of the United Farmers of Alberta. I wonder if he read the remarks of the Premier of Alberta in yesterday's Journal. He quoted from that paper yes-

Grain Board-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
fcerday, but possibly he did not see that little statement by Mr. Reid in which he said the farmers would welcome the bill. He laid great stress on the fact that Argentina is selling more wheat than Canada, and also Australia. That statement was applauded by hon. members opposite; they seemed to be pleased to hear it. What are the facts in connection with Argentine wheat? It is produced at very low cost, it is soft wheat, very inferior to Canadian wheat, and they can afford to sell it at 20 to 25 cents a bushel less. It is not worth within 25 cents of what Canadian wheat is. The same thing is true of Australia, and in addition to that, Australia has inflated money; the pound in British money is worth a pound and a half in Australia. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) explained that to-night. Australia was able to inflate because they are not a debtor nation as we are. They owe money, but they owe it to their own people and so inflation does not cause them any trouble. If we did not have these enormous obligations to meet in New York and elsewhere abroad, we might be able to sell more wheat. We have got to meet our obligations in the terms of the agreement, in gold.
Then the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) said: Where is that great market in France that the Prime Minister referred to? Surely the hon. member if he reads must know that France has wheat to sell, that France exported wheat last year. More than that, they grew more wheat than Canada last year, so what is the use of asking where is that great market in France? Then he talked of gambling in wheat. Well, if I can interpret gambling-and I have done a little of it on the races once in a while- when I put some money say on a horse race, I expect to make a profit. I do not think it has ever been in the mind of the Prime Minister of this country or of Mr. McFarland1 to make a profit on that wheat. All this government did was to step in and strengthen the market in order to maintain prices. We have no desire to make a profit, to gamble; that was never the intention of the government. We would be happy indeed to get out on an even keel, but if we have to take a loss, we feel the sacrifice will be worth the cost. During the darkest days we have ever experienced, we have maintained one of the greatest industries in Canada. Western Canada would have been bankrupt to-day-heaven knows it is bad enough-had the government not taken action; the whole country would have been in the hands of receivers. There is no question 
about that; hon. gentlemen opposite know it, if they would just forget politics long enough to admit it.
The hon. member for Willow Bunch took some time in an effort to prove that from time to time the Prime Minister has contradicted himself. My only reply to that would be that when a man ceases to change his opinions and develop new and better tastes, the jungle forces of cynicism, doubt and reaction set in. There is no crime in a man's changing his opinion in a world changing so rapidly-no crime at all. If that is the best case hon. members opposite can make out against Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, the Conservative party has very little to worry about in the next election. If what hon. members opposite have been saying against this 'bill is the best case they can make out, then I pity them when they go to their people.
It is true that I have received telegrams from western Ganada opposing the bill. I do not know whom they were from; I would not know the senders from a load of hay, nor do I want to know them. I have received no telegrams from my own constituents, and those are the only people to whom I will pay attention. They appear to be satisfied. My constituency was one of the few in Manitoba to support the egg and poultry .pool. They had intelligence enough to do that, and they will have intelligence enough to recognize the merit in this measure. So far as I am concerned they may continue to wire me all they like. My belief is that those telegrams were inspired by people opposed to the bill and who would like to continue to fleece the farmer .as thejr have been doing for the last fifty years without any regard to his position.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to continue the debate at this late hour of the evening, but there are a few observations I should like to make before the bill is given second reading. I do not believe it is necessary to cover the early history of the efforts of western farmers to improve their marketing methods. That was ably done by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon. The early efforts towards the organization of farmer's movements in western Canada culminated in she years 1923 and 1924 in the establishment of the three wheat pools. So far as their marketing operations were concerned those organizations were successful to the point of controlling roughly fifty per cent of the grain produced by the three western provinces.
In that connection may I digress for a moment. The three pool organizations,

Grain Board-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
namely Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, were separate units so far as the gathering of grain was concerned. They were collective units, however, with respect to the sale of grain in that they joined together in what is known as the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. They were also united, as I recall it, in .their financial arrangements. That is to say, the financial arrangement made with the banks was made with the central selling agency, which body, in turn, loaned the money to the .provincial pools. In establishing themselves the pools made arrangements whereby voluntary contracts were signed by the growers in which the agreement was made to deliver all the wheat grown or acquired by each grower, except such quantities as might be used for seed and feed, to the provincial pool organization for a period of five years. It was on the strength of those contracts that the pool organizations were able to finance. The banks loaned money on the strength of the contract and the whole organization was established on that basis. However when it came to the actual purchasing of the grain, beoause they did not have share capital as ordinary companies have, the pools were obliged to adopt the policy of paying initial payments to the growers and then, as the grain was sold, to advance the full amounts of money. As I recall it, the arrangements made with the banks with respect to the financing of pool operations were that the pool was required to maintain with the banks a margin of reserve of fifteen per cent.
At that time it was considered that the financial arrangement by that procedure was quite safe and sound. In making financial arrangements with the banks at the beginning of each year, of necessity the pools had to consult with the banks as to what the initial payments should be. We come to the 1928-29 crop year and the 1929-30 crop year. The financial arrangements for those crops were made by the central selling agency, and an initial payment of $1 per bushel, at Fort William, was agreed upon by the banks. Unfortunately in the fall of 1929 the market broke sharply, and the pool found difficulty in maintaining its margin. Early in the spring of 1930, shortly after the new year in fact, the margin of security which the pools had with the banks in the form of grain and collateral became jeopardized to the extent that the banks were alarmed. It was then that the pools went to their respective provincial governments, as separate units, and asked for assistance. That assistance was granted, and what took place from then on has been told on different occasions. The
banks were given a guarantee to provide for the respective shares of the different provincial organizations. In the fall of 1930 the Prime Minister went to the old country to attend an imperial conference, and he took with him the late A. J. McPhail who was then the president of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. The pool's financial difficulties were still of some considerable proportion. Upon Mr. MoPhail's return to this country, however, Mr. McFarland was appointed' general manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. The point I make is this, that from the appointment of Mr. McFarland until yesterday no statement has been made with respect to the pool's operations under his control, and at the same time there has been all kinds of confusion as to what the position actually was, for whom he was working and from whom he was taking his orders. It was generally understood that the government was guaranteeing his operations and endorsing what he was doing. However, as I have stated, until yesterday no definite statement was made.
So far as I am concerned, and I think so far as the general public is concerned, I be-'ieve no serious exception has been taken to the government coming to the assistance of the pool, and little criticism has been offered. I would be one of the last to offer any criticism for the government's coming to the assistance of the pools, because by so doing not only did it help the pools out of a difficult situation, but it helped the market for the non-pool farmers as well. I would state, further, that no government at that time could have afforded to act otherwise. Since the bill has been introduced considerable discussion has hinged around the 1929 carryover and the situation which has existed since that time. The Prime Minister even went so far as to twit the Liberal Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Malcolm), with respect to the statement he made in 1929, in regard to wheat when he said that the dominion government was not exercised over the sale of such commodities as wheat because such commodities found their own market. I do not know why the Prime Minister and others bring that up; I do not understand what they mean by so doing. It may be a nice political catch phrase, but I submit that the facts were that you had the pools controlling roughly fifty per cent of the grain crop of western Canada and you had the trade with practically an equal amount, each no doubt vying with the other in respect to price to a certain extent. The banks had already endorsed the pool's initial
