payment and were acquainted with their activities and with the activities that the trade was carrying on. Everybody was bullish at that time, and the question that always comes to my mind when that statement is repeated is, what would the Prime Minister have done under those circumstances? Would he have gone to the pool or to tlhe grain trade or to the banks or to others interested in the grain market and said: Boys, you will have to reduce your price, change your policy and sell your wheat? Even had he done so, these were private companies operating on their own, and I doubt if they would have graciously accepted any advice from an outsider. I doubt if the suggestion would have been obeyed in any respect even if it had been given.
I hesitate to refer to the statements that have been made so often by other speakers with respect to what the Prime Minister has said on previous occasions about the wheat market. I shall not do so to-night, but I should like to give one extract from an old country newspaper with respect to the preference on Canadian wheat of six cents a bushel contained in the Ottawa agreement. I quote from the Daily Herald:
The suggestion that the Ottawa tariff preference of 2s. per quarter accorded by Britain to Canadian wheat should be forfeited, on the grounds that Canada has not complied with Article 4 of the agreement, was made yesterday in the annual report of the Liverpool Corn Trade Association.
The agreement provided that the preference "may be removed if at any time empire producers ... are unable or unwilling to offer___
at prices not exceeding the world prices."
The report mentions that a deputation of British millers recently waited on the Dominion Secretary and represented that the high price asked for Canadian wheat as compared with Argentine, as a result of the Canadian government's holding policy, was in breach of this stipulation.
The report states that while the article was not-perhaps intentionally- drafted with too much precision, yet taken from one angle Canada should' have forfeited her preference long before now.
I think it is important to keep that in mind in view of the statement which has been made with respect to the marketing of wheat from this country.
Let me proceed a little further. I shall not refer to the other statements that I had in mind. Yesterday when the Prime Minister spoke he put about five acres of figures on Hansard, which to my mind confused the issue extremely. The figures went back over such a long period of time that I am afraid even my right hon. friend's friends will have difficulty in digesting them when the occasion arises. I have some figures which I have been

successful in securing, not of 1921 but as of May 17, 1935, and I should like to quote them, keeping in mind the general sales policy with respect to wheat. They are taken from the Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation dated May 17, 1935, and supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce:
Since the commencement of the present cereal year the Argentine has shipped 149 million bushels as compared with 101 million bushels during the corresponding period of 1933-34. Since August 1, 1934, Australian shipments have amounted to 91 million bushels as compared with 70 million bushels cleared during the same period in the previous crop year. Shipments from North America are sharply lower during the present crop year as compared with a year ago. From August 1, 1934, to May 13, 1935, North American shipments amounted to 127 million bushels as compared with 178 million bushels during the corresponding period of the previous crop year.
Right under that I read this:
In Liverpool, C.I.F. quotations for all classes of wheat are on about the same level as a month ago with Canadian No. 2 Northern (Atlantic shipment) now being quoted at approximately 96 cents a bushel, Argentine Rosafe at 74 cents a bushel and Australian wheat at 82 cents a bushel.
In other words, there was a spread between the Argentine and the Canadian price of 22 cents a bushel. I find an equally interesting statement on the next page:
During the present crop year the Argentine has shipped 149 million bushels of wheat as compared with 99 million bushels during the corresponding period of 1933-34. On May 12, 1935, the Argentine had 114 million bushels of wheat available for export and carry-over as compared with 167 million bushels a year ago, a reduction of 53 million bushels. If an allowance for a normal carry-over of 80 million bushels is made, the Argentine has 34 million bushels still available for export during the balance of the crop year.
Then with respect to Australia:
From August 1, 1934, to May 12, 1935, Australian "shipments amounted to 91 million bushels compared with 69 million bushels during the same period of 1933-34. On May 12, 1935, Australia had a balance of 64 million bushels available for export and carry-over as compared with 111 million bushels on the same date a year ago. If the Australian carry-over on July 31, 1935, is placed at 50 million bushels, a balance of 14 million bushels remains for export during the remaining months of the present crop year.
Then turning to the last page I find figures which are very largely the same as those quoted by the Prime Minister last night. The balance of Canadian wheat for export and carryover in 1934 is estimated at
253,960,000,	and for 1934-35, 230,499,000. But then this significant statement is made:
April exports of wheat and wheat flour were slightly larger than those of the same month

Grain Board-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
in 1934. In the nine months, August-April, however, the export movement has been 5-7 million bushels lower than that of the same months of 1933-34.
At May 1, 1935, supplies for export or carry-over were 230-5 million bushels.
That is very close to the figure which the Prime Minister gave. At the rate our present shipments are moving that would indicate that our carryover is going to be in the neighbourhood of 170,000,000 to 185,000,000 bushels. I just happened! to notice last night that for the week ended June 7, 1935, there left Canada 1,315,000 bushels of wheat; in June, 1934, 18,000,000 bushels went out; June, 1933, 16,000,000; June, 1932, 15,000,000; June, 1931, 20,000,000; June, 1930, 18,000,000. That compares with 1,315,000 for the week ending June 7, 1935. Multiply that by four and you have a little over five million bushels going out during the month of June, 1935. You would have to multiply your shipments per week by ten in order to compare with previous year's shipments for the month of June.
The Prime Minister went to considerable trouble to place on record' different figures. I think he would have been fairer if he had given the position with respect to Australia and the Argentine. He put on record that Russia's production had reached over one billion bushels in one year and that the United States average yearly production exceeded 800 million bushels. In checking over the figures it will be noticeable that in one year only Russia exceeded a billion bushels. In the case of the United1 States while it is true that the average over a long period of years has been more than 800 million bushels, for 1933 their crop was 528 million bushels and for 1934, only 496 million bushels. For these last two years they have had practically only half a crop and Canada has been in much the same position. Our position in the world with respect to grain movements should be better than it is.
Australia and the Argentine have adopted an aggressive selling policy with the result that their bins are empty, whereas considerable wheat has been left on the north American continent. Both the United States and Canada have had two short -crops but we are holding the bag as far -as the carryover is concerned. We regret to think of other countries having severe drought conditions but the fact remains that it has been a blessing to us that the United States had the misfortune of losing most of her crop last year and the year before. The net result is that most of the wheat carryover is in Canada.
One might ask the reason for this discrepancy in the sales of Canadian and Australian wheat. There is no doubt that our price relationship has been out of line. This afternoon the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmoutlh put on record certain figures with regard to the price discrepancies between Argentine, Australian and Canadian wheat. I shall not repeat these figures in full but I should like to give them with respect to the fall months during which we do our heaviest shipping. The average premium of Canadian No. 2 northern ex Atlantic c.i.f. Liverpool, for the four months September 1 to December 31, over Argentine and Australian wheat was as follows:

To me these figures are significant, particularly when one considers that the logical time for wheat to move into export position in large quantities is in the fall months. Some (Observations have been made with respect to the selling policy for this country, and I would direct attention to the statement made recently by the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). That statement was put on record this afternoon and I shall not repeat it in full. This is one matter which should be looked into very carefully, the rumour that a prejudice is growing up against Canadian wheat in the importing countries, particularly Great Britain. I do not know whether these rumours are correct but I think they should be investigated. Another reason for the advantage of the Argentine in the selling of wheat is the condition to which the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) referred this afternoon, the difference in exchange. The policy in the Argentine with respect to wheat has been such that they have been able consistently to sell their wheat in the world market and at the same time give a price to their farmers which has allowed them a greater purchasing power in their own country than is given to the farmers in this country. There is another matter to be considered, one to which the Prime Minister alluded the other evening. There is a growing disposition among countries to want to trade goods for goods. The sooner this method of trading is appreciated by this and other countries of the world, the sooner we will arrive at a reasonable basis of doing business.
I should like to deal now with the bill itself. If this bill is to be put into effect

Grain Board-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he include a provision whereby the board will be required to make a report to some responsible body. As :I see it, there is nothing in this bill to require this board to report to anyone. In this connection I should like to refer to the grain control board of the Argentine and quote from a publication of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, as follows:
Just as the month of November closed, the ministry of agriculture gave publicity to the long expected statement as to the operations of the grain control board in respect of wheat.
I notice th'at this board has made a very detailed report with respect to its operations. For instance, it gives the monthly purchases, sales and cancellations and shows the stocks on hand at the end of each month. It then lists the expenses of the board, which are more than covered by the profits. It was originally estimated that there would be a loss of 50 million pesos on the operations of the board, but this did not occur. There is a final announcement by the Minister of Agriculture that the board will be in operation for another year. If the country is going to foot the bills for this board it has a right to expect some kind of report. I would also direct the attention of the Prime Minister to section 7 of the bill, which reads:
(b) to buy and sell wheat and, without restricting the generality of. such powers, to acquire from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat-
I submit that we have a right to know what obligations are to be taken over by this organization. I believe hon. members will remember the representations which I made with respect to certain operations in wheat in Manitoba. Personally I feel that this section cannot be allowed to pass without our receiving detailed information. I am not going to burden the house with full details, but I believe the Prime Minister will recall that representations were made with respect to the durum wheat handled by the Manitoba pool and then taken over by the central selling agency. In 1030-31 the pool accepted durum and common wheat from the growers at different prices. An initial payment was made of 70 cents per bushel for No. 1 northern and 64 cents per bushel for No. 1 durum. These prices were later reduced to 50 cents for No. 1 northern and 49 cents for No. 1 durum, but most of the wheat was accepted at 54 cents a bushel. The point in connection with it is this, that the durum wheat of that crop year was practically all sold at a substantial profit. It was estimated that it

brought in the neighbourhood of 67 cents a bushel, so that these people feel that they have a just claim against someone, and it is in this arrangement now that Mr. McFarland has been directing.

I do submit, however, that the bill should have been introduced earlier in the session. The situation to-day is this. The farmers thought they had sold their last year's crop, and though it is true that they disposed .of it, they now find that there is about 200,000,000 bushels of it still in this country in competition with the crop they have just sown. There is prospect of a crop of 400,000,000 bushels this year, and we are glad that conditions have changed somewhat to make that possible. Under existing circumstances, and in view of the fact that the government is interested

Grain Board-Mr. Mackenzie King
in the wheat already on hand and that that wheat is going to be a factor in the marketing of next year's crop, I frankly do not see how any government could get away from establishing some organization in the form of a board or whatever you may call it to meet the present emergency. At the same time I would hesitate very much to endorse a proposition whereby, at this stage of the game, a permanent compulsory pool 'Organization or board should be established and set in motion to conduct the wheat marketing affairs of the country for years to oome.
I dislike to see the government go into the grain marketing business. I doubt if it is sound in principle and I hate to see it established. We had an effort on the part of the pool organizations in the west, to which I referred earlier, to establish a one hundred per cent pool which would have been a compulsory organization. The effort failed. We had also an attempt to establish voluntarily a coarse grain pool, but that was not successful. And recently we had a vote taken in connection with the poultry plebiscite, which certainly was not a very satisfactory vote, so far as compulsory pooling in Manitoba at any rate was concerned.
The whole situation is involved to such an extent that I doubt very much whether you will find1 the rank and file of the farmers very enthusiastic about being committed to a compulsory grain marketing organization. That I judge to be true of Manitoba at least. There is one other feature which perhaps should1 not be mentioned, but it is a fact nevertheless. A good many farmers in Manitoba consider that they have an advantage in marketing grain in that their harvesting period is usually earlier, thus allowing them to sell on an earlier, which is often a stronger, market. That may' be selfishness, but it is nevertheless a fact to be taken into consideration when judging human nature. With respect to coarse grains, that would affect mostly Manitoba. Over half the barley is normally produced in Manitoba, so that a coarse grain pool would be of considerable interest there. Again I say that past experience has shown that the initial payments on these grains are so small as to make it impossible under existing conditions for people to carry on, and I am afraid' there will not be much enthusiasm for a coarse grain pool. It did not work when tried before. My feeling at the moment is that if we could establish a grain board which would be in a position to take offers when the market fell below a certain point, and when the market was above that figure for everyone interested in the handling of grain to be free to market
in whatever way they saw fit, we would have the most satisfactory arrangement.
I confess that I cannot see that this organization as proposed at the present time will meet with very general favour in Manitoba. From the reports I have been receiving I am inclined to think there is a good deal of opposition to it. At the same time everyone knows that the situation at present cannot continue with any degree of satisfaction or certainly without some governmental assistance. And so I would vote for the second reading of the bill on the ground that the Prime Minister has indicated that it will go to a special committee where we can look into all the questions affecting the marketing of grain, and probably from that committee there would emerge a measure that would be satisfactory to all concerned. It is too important to become a mere political issue.

speechtext: Before the Prime Minister concludes the debate, I wish to make perfectly sure that- we have a correct understanding of the situation. I believe it is understood that the bill will, after second reading, go to a committee and that the Prime Minister when he speaks will indicate whether it will be a special committee or one of the select standing committees of the house. In supporting the second reading to this end, it is understood that the opposition is not thereby committed to any of the provisions of the bill, beyond the establishment of a grain board, with such powers as may be agreed upon. In other words, we support the second reading on the understanding that we reserve our right to propose without prejudice any amendment in committee.
